procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants approached the Supreme Court because of Government intervention in issuing an Ordinance. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. Das J. agreed with the Chief Justice.

issue.issue_text: Whether the defendants' counter-claim for damages, based on the plaintiffs' failure to insure goods that were later destroyed in an explosion, was barred by an Ordinance that prohibited legal proceedings for compensation for loss arising out of the explosion.

facts: The defendants instructed the plaintiffs (their agents) to insure goods, but the plaintiffs failed to do so.
The goods were subsequently destroyed in an explosion.
An Ordinance was passed which barred legal proceedings for compensation for any loss arising out of the explosion.
The defendants filed a counterclaim against the plaintiffs for damages, arguing that the plaintiffs' failure to insure caused them to lose the value of the goods.
law: Section 18(2) of the Ordinance prohibited any suit or legal proceeding for compensation or damages for any loss of property "due to or in any way arising out of the explosion".
application: The Court distinguished between the legal basis of the defendants' claim (the cause of action) and the event that caused the physical loss of the goods.

The Court determined that the defendants' cause of action was not the explosion itself, but rather the plaintiffs' "misconduct of the agent in the business of agency"—specifically, their breach of duty for failing to insure the goods as instructed.
The Court reasoned that this claim for breach of an agent's duty did not "arise out of the explosion" in the sense meant by the Ordinance.

The explosion and the Ordinance were relevant only to calculating the amount (quantum) of damages resulting from the plaintiffs' breach of duty, but the quantum of damages is not part of the cause of action itself.
The cause of action was complete based on the duty to insure, the failure to perform that duty, and the resulting loss to the defendants.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the counterclaim was barred. It held that the defendants' claim was based on the plaintiffs' breach of their duty as agents, not on a right to compensation for loss arising from the explosion, and therefore was not prohibited by the Ordinance.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the defendants' counter-claim for damages, based on the plaintiffs' failure to insure goods that were later destroyed in an explosion, was barred by an Ordinance that prohibited legal proceedings for compensation for loss arising out of the explosion.
appellant_arguments: The defendants' (respondents') counterclaim for damages was barred by a Government Ordinance which prohibited legal proceedings for compensation for any loss arising from the explosion.
respondent_arguments: The claim was not for loss arising directly from the explosion, but for damages resulting from the appellants' breach of duty as commission agents in failing to insure the goods as instructed.
Under Section 212 of the Indian Contract Act, an agent is liable to compensate their principal for the direct consequences of their own neglect.
The appellants' failure to insure the goods was a neglect of duty, and the respondents should be placed in the same position as if the appellants had fulfilled their obligation to insure.

cases.principle: If an agent was instructed to insure goods and neglected to do so, he was liable to the principal for their value in the event of their being lost.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An agent's liability for a breach of duty, such as failing to insure goods as instructed, arises from the misconduct itself. A subsequent, unforeseeable legislative act that quantifies the damages resulting from that breach does not create a new liability or break the chain of causation. The unforeseeability of the extent of the damages is not a defense if the loss flows directly from the breach of duty.
obiter: The cause of action for an agent's misconduct is completed by the existence of a duty, the failure to perform that duty, and the resulting damage; the quantum of the damages is not a part of the cause of action.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the Ordinance did not bar the defendants' counterclaim because the legal cause of action was not the loss from the explosion, but rather the plaintiffs' breach of their duty as agents in failing to insure the goods. This breach of duty occurred prior to and independent of the explosion. The Ordinance did not extinguish this pre-existing liability for misconduct; it merely provided a new framework for quantifying the damages that directly flowed from that breach.
legal_tests_applied: An agent is liable to make compensation to his principal for the direct consequences of his own neglect, want of skill, or misconduct, but not for losses that are indirectly or remotely caused by such neglect (based on Section 212 of the Indian Contract Act).
Analysis of the true cause of action, distinguishing between the legal basis for a claim (breach of duty) and the event that triggers the materialization of loss (the explosion).
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellants' contention that the respondents' claim was for loss arising from the explosion; instead, it found the claim was based on the appellants' breach of duty in the business of the agency.

The court determined that the appellants' liability arose not from the Ordinance, but from their failure to insure the goods as instructed, a breach of duty that was separate from and unaffected by the Ordinance.
The argument that the extent of liability was unanticipated was dismissed as no defense in law, as the damages were found to flow directly from the breach of duty.
why_respondent_won: The respondents successfully established that their cause of action was the appellants' misconduct in failing to insure the goods, which was a complete cause of action separate from the explosion.

The court accepted that the appellants' misconduct gave rise to a liability to make good the damage and to put the respondents in the same position they would have been in if their goods had been insured.

The court agreed that the Ordinance did not create a new liability or bar the existing one, but rather served as the 'yardstick' for quantifying the damages resulting from the appellants' pre-existing breach of duty.
